messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The study is a comparative LCA/LCC of multiple technologies (single-use AER, regenerable AER, single-use GAC, GAC with thermal regeneration) using the same contaminated water flow (6000 L/hr for each system) and a 30‑year system life cycle (S11-E06, S11-E08). This supports that results are comparable, with conditions related to shared assumptions and modeled nature of the systems.

The source supports that systems are compared on a consistent basis for environmental impacts and costs over a 30‑year life cycle and at a common flow rate (S11-E06, S11-E08). However, the record explicitly states the use of the same PFAS-impacted groundwater and a consistent breakthrough-criterion framework for all systems; while consistent breakthrough criteria are discussed broadly (S11-E01, S11-E05), this is not spelled out as an identical framework across all systems in the provided text, so part of the justification is inferred rather than directly stated.

The endpoint concerns modeled media usage rate (MUR) and sorbent burn rate, which are process/operational metrics rather than removal efficiency, destruction, or mineralization. Classifying the endpoint_type as "other" is appropriate given the LCA/LCC context (S11-E01, S11-E06).

The conclusion notes that environmental impacts and costs are most sensitive to MUR and that stringent breakthrough criteria greatly increase MUR (S11-E01). Table text shows a Sorbent Burn Rate metric (S11-E06). The abstract/conclusion also states that high impacts for GAC result from high MUR and that impacts can be reduced when GAC is thermally reactivated (S11-E08). Together these support the interpretation that the model calculates MUR and sorbent burn rate for GAC and that high MUR leads to relatively high environmental impacts, partially mitigated by reactivation.

This endpoint describes comparative life cycle environmental impacts across technologies, which is a modeled LCA outcome rather than a direct treatment performance metric; classifying it as "other" fits the schema (S11-E08, S11-E01).

The text states that single-use GAC had the highest emissions and treatment costs, and that thermally reactivated GAC was less impactful than regenerable AER but still more impactful than single-use PFAS-selective AER, which had the lowest environmental impacts and costs (S11-E08). The conclusion highlights incineration of wastes as a primary source of environmental impact, and mentions thermal reactivation and reuse of GAC as a way to minimize quantities of waste sent for disposal (S11-E01). This supports the interpretation given, including the role of incineration and regeneration-related processes in impacts.
The endpoint is life cycle treatment cost per volume treated, a cost metric from LCC rather than a removal/destruction endpoint; classifying as "other" is appropriate (S11-E04).

Table values show cost per m³: single-use resin $0.28, regenerable resin $0.40, single-use GAC $0.50, and GAC with Thermal Regen $0.44 (S11-E04). This matches the interpretation that LCC estimates cost per cubic meter for GAC with thermal regeneration, lower than single-use GAC but higher than single-use PFAS-selective AER under the baseline scenario.

The record correctly infers that this is a modeled LCA/LCC study, not direct long-term full-scale measurements; the abstract and title describe an LCA/LCC using field pilot data to inform model inputs (S11-E08), and off-site regeneration is modeled (S11-E06). Thus, describing the limitation as reliance on assumed/media usage rates, breakthrough criteria, and off-site regeneration practices informed by field and literature data is a reasonable, design-inferred limitation.

The title and introduction refer to remediation of groundwater contaminated by PFASs (S11 title, S11-E07). The systems are modeled rather than observed full-scale operations (S11-E08). Describing the matrix as "PFAS-impacted groundwater (modeled)" aligns with this evidence.
The text states: "Assumes treatment of 6000 L/hr of contaminated water through each system under the baseline scenario" (S11-E06), matching the value 6000 for flow rate.
The flow rate is given in L/hr in the text ("6000 L/hr", S11-E06), so unit "L/hr" is correct.

S11-E06 explicitly describes Remediation System 2 (regenerable AER) as "a lead-lag series of adsorber vessels". The same chunk indicates that each remediation system treats 6000 L/hr, but does not explicitly state that the GAC systems also use a lead-lag configuration in the provided text. It is plausible and likely from the full paper that GAC is also lead-lag, but this is not directly shown in the supplied excerpt; thus, the claim that GAC is operated in a similar lead-lag configuration is partially inferred.
This operating condition is a descriptive configuration ("lead-lag adsorber vessels"), not a numeric quantity; leaving the unit null is appropriate.

The table footnote states: "Base case scenario assumed where changeout criteria is dictated by PFSA detection" (S11-E06). The conclusion further discusses more stringent breakthrough criteria such as detection of any PFASs in effluent (S11-E01), and S11-E05 discusses how breakthrough criteria (definition of PFAS breakthrough) affect impacts and costs. Together this supports the stated value of PFSA detection in effluent as the baseline media changeout criterion.
The media changeout criterion is a qualitative description (PFSA detection in effluent), so it is appropriate that no unit is given.

The table excerpt states: "GAC thermal regeneration is operated as hazardous at an offsite facility" and distinguishes this from incineration of single-use media (S11-E06). This supports the value "off-site thermal reactivation" for management of spent GAC media.
Management of spent media is described qualitatively; no unit is needed, so a null unit is appropriate.

The abstract notes that sensitivity analyses highlighted the dominance of MUR for impacts and costs over a "30-year system life cycle" (S11-E08). This supports the use of 30 years as the system lifetime in LCA/LCC modeling.
The system lifetime is in years ("30-year system life cycle", S11-E08), so the unit "years" is correct.

S11-E05 notes that contaminated sites are typically associated with many different PFASs, particularly AFFF-impacted groundwater, and that breakthrough criteria vary depending on how PFAS breakthrough is defined. S11-E04 references regulated PFAS analytes. This supports the description that multiple PFASs are present and that media changeout criteria depend on regulated analytes and chosen breakthrough definitions.
The cost table lists "GAC with Thermal Regen" with cost per m³ of $0.44 (S11-E04). The recorded value 0.44 matches this exactly and is marked as an exact numeric value.

The table notes that cost per m³ is determined by combining annual capital and operational costs divided by volume of water treated (S11-E04), implying a unit of USD per m³. The unit "USD/m3" is therefore correct.

The descriptive qualifier that this is a modeled life cycle treatment cost per cubic meter under baseline assumptions (combining annualized capital and operating costs) aligns with the table note describing cost per m³ as annual capital plus operational cost divided by annual treated volume (S11-E04).

S11-E06 states that GAC thermal regeneration is operated as hazardous at an offsite facility, implying transport and high-temperature processing of spent media. S11-E01 identifies incineration of wastes as a primary source of environmental impact and describes how thermal reactivation and reuse of GAC can minimize waste sent for disposal. While emissions and residue handling are not quantified in the excerpt, it is a reasonable design inference that combustion emissions and regeneration residues contribute to environmental impacts, supporting this limitation description.

S11-E01 explicitly states that incineration of wastes is a primary source of environmental impact and that thermal reactivation and reuse of GAC reduce waste quantities sent for disposal. However, the text does not explicitly frame high-temperature treatment steps associated with GAC regeneration itself as a primary contributor on par with incineration; this is partially inferred. Thus, the mention of incineration as a primary contributor is supported, while inclusion of GAC regeneration as a primary contributor is somewhat stronger than the direct wording.

The title and abstract describe a life cycle assessment and life cycle cost analysis of AER and GAC systems using field pilot data to inform model inputs (S11 title, S11-E08). GAC thermal regeneration is modeled as being operated at an offsite hazardous facility (S11-E06). This supports describing the study as a system-level LCA/LCC model of GAC adsorption with off-site thermal regeneration for PFAS-impacted groundwater, parameterized with field pilot data.

The title and abstract identify the work as a life cycle assessment and life cycle cost analysis (S11 title, S11-E08). Classifying the study type as "modeling_or_life_cycle_study" is therefore accurate.

The provided text confirms that GAC systems are compared as adsorption treatment systems for PFAS-contaminated groundwater and that GAC thermal regeneration is operated as hazardous at an offsite facility, enabling reuse of GAC (S11-E06, S11-E08). However, the supplied excerpts explicitly describe a lead-lag configuration only for regenerable AER (S11-E06) and do not directly state that GAC is also in lead-lag vessels in the visible text. Thus, the general description of GAC adsorption with offsite thermal regeneration and reuse is supported, but the specific claim of lead-lag vessels for GAC is partially inferred.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements for synthesis—study identity, PFAS-impacted groundwater matrix, GAC adsorption with off-site thermal regeneration, LCA/LCC endpoints, key operating conditions (flow rate, lifetime, management of spent media), and quantitative cost per m³—are directly supported by the cited text. Some configuration details (lead-lag for GAC) and attributions of impact contributions (explicitly including regeneration as a primary contributor) are partially inferred, but these do not compromise the main quantitative and comparative findings. The record is therefore usable with minor qualifiers on those partially supported details.
